voice-surgery-cricothyroid-approximation.summary: Surgery that draws the laryngeal cartilages together to tension the vocal folds and raise speaking pitch, mainly used for voice feminisation.

quick.overview:
Cricothyroid approximation (CTA) is a voice surgery that raises your speaking pitch. The payoff people want is a higher voice, and the pitch change is measurable after surgery. It has mainly been used for voice feminisation in transgender women.

The surgeon moves the cricoid and thyroid cartilages closer together, which lengthens and tenses the vocal folds. A 2017 systematic review of pitch-raising surgery found mixed results, and a 2025 meta-analysis reported that surgery generally produced larger and more lasting pitch gains than voice therapy. Fewer clinicians perform CTA now than Wendler glottoplasty.
quick.how: CTA is performed by a surgeon as a one-off operation, not a routine you repeat. It is sometimes considered by people for whom voice therapy has not given enough change. Newer techniques have largely replaced it, so availability is limited.
quick.risks: It is irreversible surgery. Reported risks include a voice locked into falsetto, loss of loudness or quality, swallowing or breathing problems, infection and scarring, and outcomes may decline over time.

angle.text: Cricothyroid approximation pulls the laryngeal cartilages together to tension the vocal folds, giving a higher speaking pitch that can be measured after surgery. It has mainly been used for voice feminisation, and newer techniques have largely replaced it.

adam-s-apple-enhancement.summary: Surgical enlargement of the Adam's apple to give the neck a more prominent, masculine profile, described mostly within facial masculinization.

quick.overview:
Adam's apple enhancement enlarges the bump at the front of the neck, which is usually more pronounced in men, to give a more masculine neckline. The change is directly visible in the neck profile.

A surgeon adds volume over the thyroid cartilage, with a custom implant or cartilage work. It appears in the literature mainly as part of facial masculinization surgery for transmasculine patients, alongside mandible angle and chin procedures. One 2025 report followed six patients who received personalized PEEK implants planned from scans.
quick.how: It is done as a surgical procedure, often alongside other facial masculinization work such as jaw and chin changes. Results are visible once the surgical swelling settles.
quick.risks: It is surgery near the larynx, so complications are possible. The published series is small (six patients), so complication rates are not established.

angle.text: Surgical enlargement of the Adam's apple adds a visible prominence at the front of the neck for a more masculine profile. It is described mainly as part of facial masculinization for transmasculine patients, in small case series.

neck-training-for-voice.summary: Neck training with the aim of thickening the neck and, according to some in looksmaxxing circles, deepening the voice.

quick.overview:
Some people in looksmaxxing communities train the neck hoping for a thicker-looking neck and a deeper voice. The neck-size payoff is the part most people can see.

Proponents reason that thicker neck muscles change how the neck and larynx work and so lower the voice. No published studies test the voice claim, and standard sources attribute pitch mainly to vocal fold size and laryngeal growth.
quick.how: People add neck exercises to a regular strength routine and track neck size over months. It is usually combined with general lifting.
quick.risks: No specific risks were documented for the voice claim. Heavy neck exercise carries general injury risks.

angle.text: The aim is a thicker neck and, per forum claims, a deeper voice as neck muscles grow and change how the larynx sits and works. No published studies test the voice part.

hydration-and-humidifier-for-voice.summary: Drinking water and humidifying the room to keep the vocal folds moist for a clearer, less fatigued voice.

quick.overview:
Drinking water and running a humidifier are used to keep the voice clear, smooth and less tired. The payoff people want is a voice that holds up through long talking or singing.

Proponents say moisture lubricates the vocal folds, and humidifiers add moisture to the air. One small study of karaoke singers looked at hydration together with vocal rest in relation to vocal fatigue.
quick.how: People keep water through the day and run a humidifier in dry rooms, often overnight or in winter. It is an everyday habit rather than a course with an end date.
quick.risks: Humidifiers can spread microorganisms if left unclean and can promote mold when humidity is too high, so they need regular cleaning.

angle.text: Water and humidified air keep the vocal folds moist, which users say means less vocal fatigue and a clearer, smoother voice. A study of karaoke singers examined hydration alongside vocal rest in relation to vocal fatigue.

throat-coat-tea.summary: Slippery-elm herbal teas such as Throat Coat, drunk for a soothed throat and a more comfortable voice.

quick.overview:
Throat Coat-style teas are drunk for a soothed throat and a clearer, more comfortable voice, especially around heavy voice use by singers and speakers.

They are commonly built around slippery elm, whose inner bark has long been used in folk medicine for sore throat and is sold in the US as an over-the-counter demulcent, a coating soothing agent. Use is traditional, and no clinical studies of these teas were found.
quick.how: People drink the tea warm before or after heavy talking or singing, as part of a wider voice-care routine alongside water and rest.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed did not describe adverse effects.

angle.text: Singers and voice-conscious users drink slippery-elm teas to soothe the throat lining, easing irritation so the voice feels clearer and more comfortable. Use is traditional and no clinical studies of these teas were found.

honey-and-ginger-throat-soothing.summary: Warm honey and ginger drinks used to soothe the throat and keep the voice comfortable.

quick.overview:
Honey and ginger in warm drinks are used to soothe a sore throat and keep the voice comfortable and easy to use.

Proponents say honey coats the throat and ginger soothes it. A Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found no strong evidence for or against honey for coughs, while the WHO recommends honey for coughs and sore throats. Ginger has a long traditional-medicine history, and its effectiveness for treating disease remains uncertain.
quick.how: People stir honey, fresh ginger or both into hot water or tea, usually when the throat feels rough or after heavy voice use.
quick.risks: Honey should not be given to infants under one because of infant botulism risk. Ginger can interact with anticoagulants.

angle.text: Honey and ginger drinks soothe a sore, irritated throat so the voice feels easier and clearer. Honey has some cough data and WHO guidance for sore throats, while ginger rests on traditional use.

vocal-rest.summary: Cutting back on talking and singing after strain so the voice recovers to a clear, steady sound.

quick.overview:
Vocal rest means reducing speaking and singing so a strained voice can recover and sound clear and steady again.

The premise is that less vocal loading lets fatigue and irritation settle. It is part of standard vocal hygiene advice for voice professionals, and vocal fatigue and recovery in singers and speakers have been studied in several small studies.
quick.how: People cut down talking, singing and shouting for a period after heavy use or when the voice feels tired, often with water and sleep.
quick.risks: No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed. Persistent voice problems are typically assessed by clinicians.

angle.text: Resting the voice after strain lets the vocal folds recover, so the voice comes back clearer and less hoarse. Vocal rest appears in vocal hygiene guidance for voice professionals and sits within research on vocal fatigue.

avoiding-whispering.summary: A voice-care habit of speaking softly in a normal voiced tone instead of whispering, to reduce strain and keep the voice sounding healthy.

quick.overview:
Avoiding whispering means using quiet voiced speech rather than a whisper when the voice is tired or hoarse, to reduce strain and protect voice quality.

Whispering keeps the vocal folds apart and makes sound from air turbulence. Proponents say people often push harder to be heard, which may add strain. Reference works note that whispering can strain the vocal cords more than regular speech for some people, sourced to a 2011 newspaper article rather than a trial.
quick.how: People speak softly and normally when resting the voice, alongside other vocal hygiene habits such as less shouting, less throat clearing and staying hydrated.
quick.risks: Few risks are attached to the habit itself. Experts generally advise medical evaluation if hoarseness lasts more than two weeks.

angle.text: Speaking softly in a voiced tone instead of whispering is meant to reduce vocal strain so the voice stays clearer and healthier-sounding. The advice appears in voice-care discussion and rests on limited evidence.

treating-acid-reflux-for-voice.summary: Managing laryngopharyngeal reflux to relieve hoarseness and get a clearer, less strained voice.

quick.overview:
People with chronic hoarseness or frequent throat clearing are sometimes evaluated for laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR, or silent reflux) and treat it to get a clearer voice.

LPR is the backward flow of stomach contents into the throat, thought to irritate the larynx and cause hoarseness and strain. Many patients have little or no heartburn. Trials of acid-suppressing drugs for LPR have shown mixed results, and the diagnosis itself is debated.
quick.how: Management commonly combines diet and lifestyle changes, medication such as proton-pump inhibitors, alginate products, and sometimes surgery, usually guided by a clinician.
quick.risks: Hoarseness has many causes, and clinicians generally recommend evaluation when it persists. PPIs have their own adverse-effect profiles, and long-term use warrants clinician involvement.

angle.text: Controlling reflux reduces irritation of the larynx, which can ease hoarseness and give a clearer voice. Treatment studies for LPR are mixed and the diagnosis is debated.

quit-smoking-for-voice.summary: Stopping smoking to avoid or ease hoarseness and the lowered, rougher voice that smoking causes through vocal fold swelling.

quick.overview:
Quitting smoking protects the voice from hoarseness and the lowered, rougher pitch linked to smoking. Smoking is described as the leading cause of Reinke's edema, a fluid buildup in the vocal folds.

Smoke exposure makes the vocal fold cover fluid-filled, so the folds get heavier and vibrate more slowly, lowering pitch and causing hoarseness. Cessation is reported to halt progression but not necessarily reverse existing swelling.
quick.how: Quitting is part of standard management for Reinke's edema, and cessation support is available through clinicians, often combined with other vocal hygiene habits.
quick.risks: Continued smoking raises the risk of precancerous changes and laryngeal cancer, and is listed as a cause of vocal fold injury. Existing swelling may not reverse after quitting.

angle.text: Stopping tobacco lets vocal fold swelling stop progressing, so the voice stays clearer and less rough and low. Smoking is a documented cause of vocal fold swelling, though studies focus on health rather than voice attractiveness.

whisky-and-cigar-voice-fad.summary: The idea that smoking and drinking give a deep, husky voice; the voice change is documented in some smokers as a sign of vocal fold disease.

quick.overview:
Some online circles associate cigars, smoking and whisky with a deep, husky voice that sounds attractive. No source reviewed documents the fad's origin.

Medical references do describe a real link between smoking and a lower, hoarse voice: smoke exposure causes fluid buildup in the vocal folds (Reinke's edema), which slows vibration, lowers pitch and causes hoarseness. The attractiveness claim rests on anecdote.
quick.how: Followers of the idea smoke or drink with the aim of getting a huskier voice over time.
quick.risks: Documented harms include laryngeal cancer risk, precancerous changes, breathing difficulty from swelling and, in some cases, surgery. The voice change reflects vocal fold disease.

angle.text: The aim is a deep, husky voice from smoke and alcohol irritating the vocal cords. The lowered voice is documented in some smokers as a result of vocal fold swelling; its attractiveness rests on anecdote.

deep-voice-masculinity-meta.summary: The belief that a lower voice reads as more masculine and dominant, lifting perceived attractiveness and status.

quick.overview:
This forum framework holds that a lower pitch signals masculinity and dominance, giving a stronger presence and higher perceived attractiveness and status.

Pitch is set by vocal fold length, mass and tension. Adult male folds are longer and thicker, giving a lower pitch on average: typical speech is about 90 to 155 Hz for males and 165 to 255 Hz for females. The sources reviewed document these voice differences but not the social effects.
quick.how: Followers focus on lowering how their voice sounds, through things like speaking lower in the natural range, recording setups or other voice-focused tactics covered elsewhere on the wiki.
quick.risks: Attempts to deepen the voice by straining or using irritants carry vocal health risks, and straining is described as a cause of vocal injury.

angle.text: Forums hold that a deeper voice reads as more masculine and dominant, adding to attractiveness and status. Voice physiology is well described, while the social-perception claim circulates mostly as anecdote.

voice-transformation-software.summary: Software that shifts voice pitch or timbre in real time or in post-processing so you sound deeper or different on calls, streams and recordings.

quick.overview:
Voice changers alter pitch or timbre so a speaker can sound deeper or more resonant in calls, streams and recordings. The change is audible immediately.

Algorithms change the amplitude, pitch and tone of the audio signal. Software versions are now very common, and cloning tools can model a particular person's voice. Sources describe general uses like anonymity and music production; its use for appearance is mostly discussed informally.
quick.how: People run it live on a microphone feed for calls and streams, or process recordings afterwards, tuning the pitch shift to taste.
quick.risks: Effects apply only to the processed audio, not your actual voice. Voice cloning is associated in reference sources with social engineering concerns.

angle.text: Voice changers shift pitch or timbre in real time or after recording, so you sound deeper or more resonant straight away on calls, streams and recordings. Use for appearance is mostly discussed informally.

podcast-mic-and-eq-boost.summary: A close directional mic plus low-end EQ makes recordings of your voice sound deeper, warmer and fuller.

quick.overview:
Pairing a close, directional microphone with a low-frequency EQ boost makes a recorded voice sound deeper, warmer and more resonant. The effect is audible straight away on recordings.

Directional microphones such as cardioids boost bass when the source is very close, called the proximity effect, which radio announcers are often said to use for an authoritative tone. EQ is a separate, electronic adjustment of frequency balance that can add more low end.
quick.how: People speak close to a directional mic and apply a low-end boost in the recording software, often for podcasts, streams and voice messages.
quick.risks: No health risks are documented. The effect exists only in the recording or broadcast, and the speaker's live voice is unchanged.

angle.text: A close directional mic adds bass through the proximity effect, and a low-end EQ boost adds more, so recordings sound deeper, fuller and more resonant. Your own voice stays the same.

accent-training.summary: Coaching in the sounds, stress and rhythm of a target accent so you are understood more easily and come across as more polished.

quick.overview:
Accent training teaches the sounds, stress, rhythm and intonation of a target accent so speakers are understood more easily and come across as clearer and more polished.

Speech coaches, acting coaches and linguists offer it, and speech-language pathologists do not regard accents as disorders. Research on listener adaptation finds that listeners tune to accents, and a study of 1,699 listeners found that reactions to accents depended on communication context. Its effect on perceived appearance has not been studied.
quick.how: People practice target vowels, consonants, stress and intonation with feedback from a coach or recordings. Some linguists note that changing an accent fully takes years of interaction with native speakers.
quick.risks: No physical harms are documented. Some linguists warn about unrealistic expectations of how fast an accent changes.

angle.text: Practicing the sounds, stress and rhythm of a target accent makes speech clearer or closer to that accent, which feeds into how polished you come across. It takes sustained practice.

speech-pacing-apps.summary: Apps for practicing speaking speed and pauses for a steadier, calmer, more confident delivery.

quick.overview:
Pacing apps help you monitor and practice how fast and evenly you speak, aiming for a steadier, more deliberate delivery that reads as calm and confident.

Listeners form impressions from pace. Typical English speech runs at about four syllables per second, and linguist Howard Giles found that faster speakers of several English accents were rated as more competent. The apps themselves have not been tested for appearance outcomes.
quick.how: People record themselves or speak while the app tracks pace, then adjust speed and pauses over repeated sessions.
quick.risks: No harms are documented.

angle.text: Practicing speaking speed and pauses gives a steadier, more deliberate delivery, and listeners form impressions of confidence from pace. Pace and impressions have been researched in general; the apps themselves have not been tested.

public-speaking-course.summary: Structured speech training that builds confidence and delivery for a more commanding presence.

quick.overview:
Public speaking courses and clubs teach you to deliver speeches and take feedback, building confidence and delivery for a more commanding presence.

Repeated practice in front of audiences, with peer or instructor feedback, is the route. Clubs such as Toastmasters International use peer evaluation and impromptu speaking. Studies cited on Wikipedia associate teaching public speaking with greater self-confidence, though direct research on anxiety reduction is limited.
quick.how: People join a club, school class or commercial course and give speeches regularly over weeks or months.
quick.risks: No harms are documented beyond cost and time.

angle.text: Repeated practice in front of audiences lowers anxiety and sharpens delivery, so you come across with more confident presence. Confidence gains are reported for such training.

ear-training.summary: Music-style pitch-recognition practice borrowed to build awareness and control of your voice pitch.

quick.overview:
Ear training teaches you to recognise pitches, intervals, melodies and rhythms by ear. In voice discussions it is borrowed to build awareness of vocal pitch and a more intentional tone.

It is a core part of formal music education, using solfege, interval and chord recognition, rhythm exercises and apps. Its use for voice appearance is anecdotal, and no studies have tested it for attractiveness outcomes.
quick.how: People do short listening and identification exercises with apps or a teacher, then try to match and control pitch with their own voice.
quick.risks: No harms are documented.

angle.text: Learning to recognise pitches by ear gives better awareness and control of your own vocal pitch, for a more intentional voice tone. It is established for music skills and borrowed for voice.

tongue-stretching-exercises.summary: Tongue stretches that forum posters say lower the voice; the only trial found studied them for swallowing after stroke.

quick.overview:
Tongue stretching exercises involve extending or holding the tongue in a stretched position. Some voice-focused circles say they lower the voice.

The only trial located tested them in 25 stroke patients with swallowing difficulty: a 2019 randomized trial of a four-week program of passive tongue stretching delivered by an occupational therapist, looking at tongue motility and oromotor function. No study has tested whether they change voice pitch.
quick.how: People stretch and hold the tongue out by themselves or with assistance, as a short daily practice.
quick.risks: No adverse effects were described in the available abstract, and no safety data exist for the voice-related use.

angle.text: Forum posters say stretching the tongue changes the vocal tract and lowers the voice. The only trial found studied tongue stretching in stroke patients with swallowing difficulty, not voice pitch.

gym-and-loud-lifting-for-voice.summary: A folk belief that weight training, especially grunting or shouting while lifting, deepens the voice.

quick.overview:
This is a folk belief in voice-focused corners of appearance culture that lifting weights, especially while grunting or shouting, lowers the voice.

Believers point to strength training and testosterone, or to loud vocalizing under load as practice. No published study located has tested it. Adult speaking pitch is typically about 90 to 155 Hz in men and 165 to 255 Hz in women.
quick.how: People lift and make loud sounds under load as part of their training sessions.
quick.risks: Voice therapy guidance lists yelling and forceful phonation as phonotraumatic behaviors that vocal hygiene approaches advise reducing.

angle.text: The belief is that grunting and shouting under load, along with strength training, deepens the voice. No published study located has tested it.
